peek: An infected whose tongue pulls a survivor toward him.
full_text: The cough and the drifting green trails say a Smoker has spawned, and its tongue shows where it is. While it is dragging someone it stands still and takes extra damage in campaign, so one headshot ends it. If the tongue pulls the victim against an obstacle it starts choking them, so cut it fast.

peek: An infected that pounces on whoever is on their own.
full_text: A Hunter goes for whoever is on their own, and a long pounce does damage before the clawing starts. There is about a second to shove it out of the air. A pounce does not end on its own, so a teammate has to shove it off.

peek: An infected that rides a survivor and steers them into trouble.
full_text: The Jockey's laugh is the warning. Step backwards as it jumps and it sails past, then shove and kill it. Its damage is slow; the danger is where it steers you, which is into a witch, into acid, into a tank you were not ready for, or off a ledge.

peek: An infected whose vomit sends a horde at you.
full_text: A Boomer's vomit is not damage, it is a horde sent to you, and killing it at close range coats you anyway because it bursts. Shove first, then shoot. Being biled makes you glow to both teams.

peek: An infected whose acid puddle burns worse the longer it sits.
full_text: The Spitter's green puddle burns worse the longer it has been down, and one spit can take most of a survivor's health. Moving out of it is always right, even onto worse ground, including when you are picking someone up.

peek: An infected that cannot steer once it commits to a charge.
full_text: Shoving does nothing to a Charger; only explosives stumble it. Once it commits to the charge it cannot steer, so step aside and let it hit a wall. Near water, a ledge, or a bunched-up team it flings everybody.

peek: The system behind the spawns; nothing about them is fixed.
full_text: Nothing about the spawns is fixed, and the Director decides them. Hordes of ten to thirty commons come at you every one to four minutes, from behind or off to the side, while tanks and witches only appear at threat spots the map author placed. After a heavy fight it goes quiet for roughly thirty to forty-five seconds, and that pause is the healing window.

peek: A thrown jar that pulls the horde to where it lands.
full_text: A bile bomb is crowd control, not a weapon. Wherever the jar lands pulls the horde for about twenty seconds, and any infected caught in it gets attacked by its own side. Throw it well away from the team before starting a crescendo, or to buy a route past a tank.

peek: A switch that removes teammate outlines and item glow on any difficulty.
full_text: Realism is a separate switch that works on any difficulty. It means no outlines around your teammates, no item glow, no rescue closets, and commons shrug off body shots, so it is headshots, melee, or the magnum. Learn a map with Realism off first.

peek: Your core attributes; they decide which perks you can take.
full_text: You start with one in everything and 21 to spend, so 28 in total, which is much less than earlier Fallouts. Bobbleheads and magazines raise attributes, and each level-up lets you put the point into a SPECIAL stat instead of a perk. Your SPECIAL values are what decide which perks you can take at all.

peek: What a level-up point buys; the perk chart replaced skills.
full_text: The perk chart replaced skills. Every level gives one point, and it buys either a rank of a perk or a rank of the SPECIAL attribute that unlocks deeper perks in that column. Magazines scattered around the world grant extra perks that cost no points at all.

peek: A targeting mode that slows time so you can call shots, for action points.
full_text: V.A.T.S. is a targeting system that lets you pause into a slowed-down view to line up called shots at an enemy's head, legs or weapon, in exchange for action points. Using it spends AP, which drains a power armor's fusion core faster.

peek: The core that runs power armor and drains as it is worn.
full_text: Power armor runs on a fusion core that drains with time, and faster with anything that spends AP, such as sprinting or V.A.T.S. When it empties you can still walk, but you are over-encumbered and lose V.A.T.S. and steady aim.

peek: A healing item that restores a share of your health and repairs crippled limbs.
full_text: A stimpak heals a share of your health rather than a flat amount, and repairs crippled limbs. The Medic perk is what makes them worth carrying, taking the heal from 30% up to 100% across its ranks. In Survival mode a stimpak takes fifty seconds to work instead of five, and it starts having weight.

peek: A starred enemy that heals itself fully at about half health.
full_text: A legendary enemy has a star beside its name and is otherwise an ordinary creature with a much deeper health bar. At around half health it heals itself completely and gains a new ability, so the fight is roughly twice as long as it first looks. Each one drops a weapon or armour piece carrying a random legendary effect.

peek: Fast irradiated former humans that rarely travel alone.
full_text: Feral ghouls are irradiated former humans, fast, and they almost never travel alone. The head is the reliable weakness, and taking a leg off one stops it attacking altogether. They lie among rubble playing dead and climb out of ductwork and windows, so a room that looks clear often is not.

peek: Items you scrap at a crafting table into crafting components.
full_text: Almost nothing needs a schematic; the recipes are known by default. What you need is components, which come from scrapping junk at a crafting table, from scrapping world objects such as trees and cars inside a settlement you own, or from merchants. Early on it is worth grabbing every piece of junk you can carry, not just weapons and armor.

peek: The hub for your maps, stats and inventory.
full_text: Fallout 4 begins with your character's Pip-Boy as the hub for maps, stats and inventory. Perks gained from magazines are listed separately on it.

peek: Whether a settlement's food, water, beds and defense needs are met.
full_text: Happiness is just whether needs are met: food, water, beds and defense each have to be at least the number of settlers. Power is not part of it, though better machines need it. Higher happiness makes settlers more productive.

peek: A landmark that grants a bonus while active; only one works at a time.
full_text: Standing Stones are wilderness landmarks, thirteen in total, that grant a passive ability or buff once activated, and only one stone's effect is active at a time. The three most commonly found first are the Guardian Stones (Mage, Thief and Warrior), beside the road to Riverwood. You can change which stone is active at any time by activating a different one.

peek: A three-word dragon phrase that costs no mana, only a cooldown.
full_text: Dragon Shouts, called the Thu'um or the Voice, are three-word dragon phrases that unlock powerful effects and, unlike ordinary magic, cost no mana or stat to use, only a cooldown between casts. Tapping the shout button briefly uses only its first learned word; holding the button charges it further, unlocking a longer, stronger version once the second and third words are known.

peek: Where a dragon's soul is spent to unlock a word of a shout.
full_text: Killing a dragon lets you absorb its soul, which is spent to unlock a word of power at a word wall already found. Word walls carrying shouts are scattered through dragon lairs and dungeons, and the main quest and a few faction quests also point toward specific ones directly.

peek: Reanimated Nordic warriors sealed in barrows and tombs.
full_text: Draugr are reanimated Nordic warriors, most of whom once served the Dragon Priests, now sealed inside the barrows and tombs scattered across Skyrim. Most are immune to poison and take reduced frost damage, so a mage leaning on flame and shock spells fares better than one relying on frost. Many sleep in wall alcoves until disturbed and are briefly unable to act while climbing out to fight.

peek: Blind, feral creatures of the Dwemer ruins that hunt by sound.
full_text: Falmer were once the Snow Elves, and are now disfigured, feral creatures found living deep in Dwemer ruins. Every Falmer is completely blind and hunts by sound instead, so moving quietly or attacking from range takes real advantage of that blindness. They coat their weapons in a chaurus- or spider-venom poison that deals a burst of damage on hit.

peek: A unique item given through a quest from one of the Daedric Princes.
full_text: Daedric Artifacts are scattered through Skyrim, each a unique item tied to a quest given directly by one of the Daedric Princes rather than through an ordinary quest-giver NPC. None of these Daedric quests count as an ordinary side quest, and several can be permanently failed rather than just abandoned.

peek: Unique enchanted headgear won from a Dragon Priest.
full_text: Dragon Priest Masks are unique enchanted headgear worn by the Dragon Priests met as high-level guardian bosses inside Nordic ruins, and each mask is a one-of-a-kind reward for defeating the priest wearing it. Masks replace a helmet slot and carry a fixed enchantment rather than a random one.

peek: A skill that binds a magical effect to a weapon, armor piece or jewelry.
full_text: Enchanting lets a character bind a magical effect to a weapon, armor piece or piece of jewelry. Raising the Enchanting skill increases both how many charges a newly enchanted item holds and how strong its enchantment can be. Learning a new enchantment usually means disenchanting an existing enchanted item first to study its effect.

peek: Improving existing gear with Smithing, back to or past its original quality.
full_text: Smithing lets a character forge new weapons and armor from raw ore and hides, and separately temper existing gear to sharpen or polish it back to, or past, its original quality. A higher Smithing skill unlocks bigger improvements. A weapon or armor piece carrying an enchantment needs the Arcane Blacksmith perk before it can be tempered at all.

peek: The werewolf form: hits harder and moves faster, but no gear or spells.
full_text: As a werewolf, Beast Form can be triggered once per day for a limited window. In that form you hit far harder and move faster, and gain immunity to disease, but lose the passive bonus from resting and cannot use equipment, spells or shouts until you change back. Feeding on a fresh humanoid corpse while transformed extends the time left in Beast Form and restores health.

peek: The orange suit you change into; its charge shows on the HUD.
full_text: You change into the orange HEV suit in the locker room before the day's work. The suit's own charge, shown on the HUD next to health, does not come back on its own; you top it up at a wall-mounted suit charger.

peek: An orange wall unit that tops up the HEV suit; each holds a limited reserve.
full_text: A suit charger is an orange wall-mounted unit with a black charging cord and the HEV logo, kept separate from the white health chargers with the red cross. Each charger holds a limited reserve that does not refill once spent. When a charger's screen goes dark, it is done for good.

peek: A particle-beam gun that never reloads and can charge a shot through enemies.
full_text: The Tau Cannon, or gauss gun, is a particle beam that draws straight from the suit's uranium reserve, shared with the Gluon Gun, so it never reloads. Tap-fire sends fast yellow beams that chew through unarmoured targets. Hold the alternate fire to charge a white-hot shot that punches through several enemies or a wall and explodes on the far side.

peek: Firing the Tau Cannon's charged shot straight down to throw yourself upward.
full_text: Fire the Tau Cannon's charged shot straight down and the recoil throws you upward. This is the gauss jump, which reaches ledges nothing else does.

peek: The last weapon in the game: a continuous energy stream that drinks the uranium reserve.
full_text: The Gluon Gun pours out a continuous spiral of energy that destroys most things in seconds, and goes straight through bulletproof armour, which makes it the one gun that genuinely hurts a Gargantua. It shares the uranium reserve with the Tau Cannon and drinks it fast, so it is not a room-clearing tool. It does not work underwater.

peek: A living alien rifle that grows its own hornet ammo.
full_text: The Hivehand is the living alien rifle the Alien Grunts carry, though you cannot take one from a body. It grows its own ammo, eight hornets loaded at a time and replaced within seconds, and the primary-fire hornets home in on living targets around corners. Hornets ignore anything inorganic.

peek: A suit upgrade for Xen's gaps: crouch then jump for a long leap.
full_text: The Long Jump Module is handed to you at the end of Lambda Core, and it is the only way across Xen's floating islands. Crouch and then jump in quick succession and the suit launches you a long way forward. Take a couple of practice jumps on solid ground before the first real gap.

peek: Soldiers sent in to clean the facility out; they fight in squads.
full_text: The HECU Marines are the soldiers sent in to clean the facility out, including anyone who saw what happened. They fight in squads, keep in touch by radio and throw grenades to flush you out of cover. Where they have dug in they add laser tripmines, sentry guns and manned emplacements.

peek: A three-legged, one-eyed enemy in packs that charge a sonic shockwave.
full_text: A Houndeye is three-legged with one big compound eye, and always in a pack of up to four. Together they charge a sonic shockwave that hurts you and smashes crates and glass, and the damage rises with the size of the pack. Kill the leader and the rest lose the ability to charge the wave.

peek: A six-metre armoured enemy immune to ordinary bullets.
full_text: A Gargantua is six metres of blue armour with one glowing eye, immune to ordinary bullets and a little faster than you on foot. It cooks anything close with the flame jets in its hands. You are not meant to shoot it down; if you must, only explosives and energy weapons hurt it: rockets, satchel charges, the Gluon Gun.

peek: What you spend and carry; it stays in your Shade when you die.
full_text: When your shell breaks you respawn at the last bench, and all your Geo stays behind in a Shade at or just before the room you died in. Die again before reaching it and a new Shade replaces the old one, Geo and all, so a big purse is a reason to go back first. The first nail upgrade costs Geo alone.

peek: What waits where you died, holding your Geo, until you beat it.
full_text: When you die, your Shade waits where you fell, holding your Geo, and your soul meter is cracked to two thirds until you deal with it. Walk back and an off-key music-box tune tells you it is near; it floats at you, swings a nail and casts whichever spells you have learned, and it dies after a handful of hits, returning the Geo and mending the meter.

peek: Equippable build items that cost notches; swap them only on a bench.
full_text: Charms are the build system: each takes a set number of notches, and you can only swap charms while sitting on a bench. Forty-five exist, though five are upgrades that replace another. Soul Catcher gives more healing fuel per hit, and Quick Focus makes healing a third faster.

peek: Charm slots; each charm takes a set number of them.
full_text: Each charm takes a set number of notches; you start with three notches and can find eight more. If a charm needs more notches than you have left you can force it in and go overcharmed.

peek: Forcing in a charm with too few notches left, so every hit you take does double damage.
full_text: If a charm needs more notches than you have left you can force it in and go overcharmed. Every hit you take then does double damage, which is fine for platforming and a bad idea in a boss room.

peek: A meter filled by nail hits, spent on healing or spells.
full_text: Every nail hit on an enemy adds soul to the round meter on the left, up to ninety-nine. Hold Focus to turn thirty-three soul into one mask of health; it takes over a second, you stand still for it, and a hit cancels it. Tap the cast button instead and the same soul fuels spells.

peek: Ore that pays for the later nail upgrades.
full_text: The nail is reforged four times in the City of Tears, from 5 damage up to 21. The first upgrade costs Geo alone, and the next three need one, two and three Pale Ore on top, six Ore in all. The Ore is scattered across the kingdom behind bosses, grubs and hidden rooms.

peek: A short dash with a brief cooldown, found in Greenpath.
full_text: The Mothwing Cloak is a short dash with a brief cooldown. It is the prize for the fight at the Lake of Unn end of Greenpath, and the early platforming and enemies in Greenpath put the dash to use. The Shade Cloak from the Abyss later upgrades the dash to pass through enemies, their attacks and the black Shade Gates.

peek: A charged horizontal flight from the ground or a wall.
full_text: The Crystal Heart is a charged horizontal flight from the ground or a wall. It is found in the mines of Crystal Peak. It is needed to cross the gap far west in the Ancient Basin.

peek: Where you rest to save, restore your masks, and swap charms.
full_text: Benches are everything: they save, restore your masks, and are the only place charms can be swapped. The map of an area only fills in as you rest at benches once you own a quill. When you die you respawn at the last bench.

peek: Finishing a flashing weak enemy for health.
full_text: Shoot a weak enemy until it flashes, then glory kill it for health. That is one part of the combat loop, alongside the chainsaw for ammo and the flame belch for armour. When an arch-vile is alive, skip the executions until it is dead, because it summons while you are locked into the animation.

peek: Burns a group so that kills while they burn give armour.
full_text: Flame belch a group and kill them burning for armour. It runs on a twenty-five second cooldown. The flame belch, ice bomb and ballista are collected at the Fortress between missions.

peek: Weak demons you chainsaw for a shower of ammo.
full_text: Chainsaw a fodder demon for a shower of ammo; the chainsaw has three fuel units, one always refilling on its own every twenty seconds, and fodder costs one, so it is never off the table. The super shotgun can take several fodder demons in one shot.

peek: Demons the chainsaw cannot be used on at all.
full_text: Heavy demons cost all three chainsaw fuel units, and the super heavies cannot be sawed at all. An arch-vile counts as super heavy, so no chainsaw. The Crucible is best saved for the super heavies in the last arenas.

peek: A hook under the super shotgun that yanks you toward a demon.
full_text: The meathook under the super shotgun's barrel is the movement tool: fire it into a demon and it yanks you to them for the blast, or across the arena for the escape. Small enemies are held in place when hooked; big ones are not, and may hit you on the way in, so be ready to jump off.

peek: A sword that kills most demons in one swing but holds only three charges.
full_text: The Crucible is a sword that kills any demon in one swing without a stagger, marauders excepted, who must be stunned first. It holds three charges, refilled only at fixed spots in the level, and one swing spends one charge whether it lands on a tyrant or an imp. Each kill returns health.

peek: A punch with limited charges that kills a pinky from any side.
full_text: The pinky is armoured in front and bare at the tail, and a blood punch kills it from any side. Spend the Crucible and blood punch charges on summoned demons for health.

peek: A locked gate to an optional, harder arena opened with a Slayer Key.
full_text: The purple gore nests behind locked Slayer Gates are optional arenas harder than anything around them; each opens with a Slayer Key hidden nearby. Clearing one pays three weapon points and an Empyrean Key. All six keys unlock the Unmaykr in the Fortress, a rapid three-orb gun that shares the BFG's ammo.

peek: Horizontal bars you grab mid-air and swing along to cross gaps.
full_text: Monkey bars are horizontal bars the Slayer grabs mid-air and swings along, first taught in Cultist Base. Approach at a run and jump toward the bar rather than at it, because grabbing happens automatically once you are close enough in the air. If a section has more than one bar in a row, commit to the whole chain rather than pausing between them.

peek: A demon that buffs everything in the arena and summons more demons.
full_text: An arch-vile is a walking buff totem: while it lives everything in the arena hits harder and moves faster, glowing red, and it summons more demons. It summons while you are locked into a glory kill or chainsaw animation, because you cannot interrupt it then. Find it first, skip the executions until it is dead, and put your heaviest ordnance into it.

peek: An operating system that slows time on demand.
full_text: The Sandevistan is an operating system rather than one more implant, and it is built around blades. It slows time on demand, and some variants add crit chance and crit damage on top. Mods extend the duration or shorten the cooldown.

peek: The melee operating system that cuts damage taken while it runs.
full_text: Berserk is the other operating system, and the melee one that does not care about time. While it runs it cuts damage taken and will not let your health fall below a quarter. Afterwards every enemy you put down returns a quarter of your maximum health.

peek: Lets you fire while sliding, dodging or dashing, and slows time when aiming.
full_text: Kerenzikov lets you fire while sliding, dodging or dashing, and aiming during any of those slows time for a couple of seconds. It has its own cooldown, so treat it as a repositioning tool rather than something to lean on.

peek: A track separate from character level, paid out by fixers for gigs.
full_text: Street Cred is a separate track from your character level, paid out by fixers for gigs, and how you finish a job changes the payout. It buys a permanent vendor discount up to 15% and unlocks better cars on the Autofixer. The good gear starts appearing around Street Cred 40, and it caps at 50.

peek: Nomad, Streetkid or Corpo; it changes your opening chapter.
full_text: Your lifepath is Nomad, Streetkid or Corpo. It changes the opening chapter, one unique side job, and dialogue options that keep turning up later on. Pick the opening you want to play rather than the one that sounds strongest.

peek: Someone who took on more chrome than they could carry.
full_text: Cyberpsychosis is what happens when someone takes on more chrome than they can carry: they stop identifying with people and start seeing them as weak and inferior. A cyberpsycho has the strength and speed all that hardware buys and no regard for their own life or anyone else's. There is no talking one down.

peek: A technician who installs cyberware.
full_text: Ripperdocs are the technicians who install cyberware, somewhere between a surgeon, a techie and a tattoo artist. Most operate legally; some will fit illegal military-grade hardware for the right price. Corporate rippers are free and spotless.

peek: A program fired from your cyberdeck at enemies or devices.
full_text: Quickhacks are programs you install in a cyberdeck and fire at enemies or devices. Each costs RAM, takes an upload time before it lands, and runs for a set duration. Combat hacks do damage, control hacks disable, covert hacks keep you undetected and cost the least, and ultimates are the strongest and the most expensive.

peek: A unique named weapon with an effect no other weapon has.
full_text: Iconic weapons are the unique named weapons, usually tied to a character or a quest rather than found in a shop. Each has an effect no other weapon has, and each can be upgraded to keep pace with your level instead of being outgrown.

peek: One of the five key attributes; it opens crafting and good cyberware.
full_text: Technical Ability is one of the five key attributes set at character creation, alongside Body, Cool, Intelligence and Reflexes. It quietly helps every build, because it opens crafting and the cyberware you actually want.

peek: An optional survival mode: you must eat, drink and sleep, and ammo has weight.
full_text: Hardcore mode can be switched on from the options at any time, and off again the same way; finishing the game with it on earns the achievement. Stimpaks and RadAway heal over time instead of instantly, ammunition has weight, and companions can die for good. You also drink, eat and sleep, and thirst climbs fastest.

peek: A flat amount subtracted from every hit, instead of a percentage.
full_text: New Vegas grades armor by Damage Threshold (DT), a flat amount subtracted from every hit, rather than the percentage-based system other Fallout games use. A lighter suit with real DT can outlast a bulkier one that has none. Check an item's DT and weight in the Pip-Boy rather than judging by how heavy or armoured it looks.

peek: One of three skills you pick at the start for fifteen points each.
full_text: You choose three tag skills for fifteen points each. The gun or two you are handed at the start is based on the skills you tagged.

peek: A book worth three permanent skill points, or four with Comprehension.
full_text: Skill books are three permanent points each, four with Comprehension, and there are about fifty-two of them. Magazines are ten points for a minute, doubled and tripled by the matching perks, and merchants sell them, so carry a few for a hard check.

peek: One of the two tallies a faction keeps; killing one of theirs in the open costs thirty.
full_text: Every town and faction keeps two separate tallies, fame and infamy, and your title with them comes from the pair. Being caught stealing costs two infamy; killing one of theirs in the open costs thirty. Wearing a faction's armour turns your standing with them neutral while it is on.

peek: Assassins who walk across the map to find you after you fall to Shunned.
full_text: Fall to Shunned with the Legion and squads of four assassins start walking across the map to find you. Anger the NCR too and Ranger squads join them.

peek: Giant orange wasps in swarms; their poison sting hurts.
full_text: Cazadores are giant orange wasps in swarms of four or more, flying fast and erratic, and their sting does more raw damage than a giant radscorpion's and three times the poison, for longer. You will not sneak past them. Cripple a wing in V.A.T.S. and one drops out of the air and slows to a crawl.

peek: Coyote bodies with rattlesnake heads, common at night and in caves.
full_text: Night stalkers are coyote bodies with rattlesnake heads, made in a lab and now everywhere at night and in caves. They leap and bite with venom weaker than a cazador's, but it stacks if several land, so treat the poison. They rattle and hiss when close, which is your warning.

peek: How you order your companions about.
full_text: You can bring one person and one of the two non-humans at once, ordered through the companion wheel. Your companions cannot use antivenom, so heal them with stimpaks from the companion wheel.

peek: Seven are hidden in the base game, each worth two thousand caps.
full_text: Seven snow globes are hidden in the base game and each is worth two thousand caps at the Lucky 38, where they go on a display stand. Finding all seven is the achievement, and selling them is optional.

peek: The green blobs enemies drop; they count as both gold and experience.
full_text: The green blobs enemies drop in Brotato are called materials, and picking one up hands over both the gold spent in the shop and the experience used to level up at the same time. Anything left uncollected when a wave ends is bagged automatically, and the bag's value is paid out a little at a time on later waves. Only fifty material blobs can exist on the ground at once.

peek: Brotato's difficulty slider, from Danger 0 up to Danger 5.
full_text: Danger level is Brotato's difficulty slider, running from Danger 0 up to Danger 5, and each step keeps every increase from the levels below it. Raising it introduces tougher enemy types earlier, and from Danger 2 onward it also starts adding Elite and Horde waves into the run. Some unlockable characters are only reachable by clearing a run at a specific danger level.

peek: A wave with one tough unique enemy that drops a Legendary item.
full_text: From Danger 2 upward, a run includes one or more Elite or Horde waves layered on top of the normal wave. Elite waves add one tough, unique enemy that will not repeat within the same run; killing it drops a guaranteed Legendary item and heals a chunk of health on pickup.

peek: A wave that throws extra enemies at you, worth less material each.
full_text: Horde waves simply throw extra enemies at you, worth less material each but more in total. They appear from Danger 2 upward, layered on top of the normal wave. Danger 4 and 5 runs see three of these harder waves instead of one.

peek: Paying to refresh the shop; the fee climbs with each reroll.
full_text: Between waves the shop can be rerolled for a fee that climbs with the wave number and with every reroll already spent that shop. Buying all four items on offer earns a free reroll. Any item can be locked to keep it in the shop at its current price.

peek: Groups items by stat or playstyle; a character's tags weight the shop.
full_text: Items are grouped by the stat or playstyle they support, such as melee damage or max health. Most characters favor a set of item tags, which weights the random shop toward items that suit how that character is meant to be played, rather than forcing any specific build.

peek: An enemy that runs away and boosts every other enemy while alive.
full_text: A Buffer runs away from the player rather than closing in, and while alive it boosts every other enemy's health, damage and speed substantially, with buffed enemies outlined in red. Killing it quickly removes a much bigger problem than its health bar suggests.

peek: An enemy that wanders the crowd restoring health to nearby enemies.
full_text: A Healer wanders among the crowd, restoring health to nearby enemies in an amount that climbs a little with every wave. It is not very tough on its own, so killing it quickly removes a much bigger problem than its health bar suggests, especially once a wave gets crowded.

peek: A weak early enemy that keeps its distance and fires projectiles.
full_text: Spitters keep their distance and fire projectiles, retreating if the player gets too close. They are one of the weak, common enemy types of the first waves. They gain a flat amount of extra health and damage every wave they remain in play.

peek: The guaranteed reward for beating an Elite wave's unique enemy.
full_text: Beating the unique enemy in an Elite wave always drops a Legendary-tier loot crate, which is guaranteed to contain a Legendary item rather than leaving it to chance like a normal crate. Picking it up also restores a set chunk of health on the spot.

peek: The item you throw at a weakened wild Pal to try to catch it.
full_text: The Pal Sphere is the basic, earliest tool for catching wild Pals, thrown at a target to attempt a capture rather than guaranteeing one. The odds depend on the sphere's own capture power, how much health the target Pal has left, and situational bonuses such as landing the throw from behind. Its capture power is comparatively low, so tougher targets call for a higher-tier sphere.

peek: The base's anchor; it sets where you can build and put Pals to work.
full_text: A base is anchored by a Palbox, whose placement sets both the base's location and the area where structures can be built and Pals put to work. Losing the Palbox destroys everything the base is built around, so protecting it matters as much as growing it.

peek: How well a Pal fits a job at your base.
full_text: Every job at a base, from crafting to cooking to construction, carries its own workload value. Pairing tasks with Pals whose Work Suitability fits the job gets things done faster than assigning whichever Pal is nearby.

peek: A structure where two Pals of opposite genders produce a Pal Egg.
full_text: Breeding lets two Pals of opposite genders produce a Pal Egg at a Breeding Farm, a structure unlocked at level nineteen that also requires clearing a specific story boss fight before it can actually be built. Once a male and female Pal are placed inside and a cake is left in the farm's chest, they begin breeding on their own, and keep going as long as cake remains.

peek: A hidden rarity tier; a lower number means a rarer, more powerful Pal.
full_text: Which species hatches is decided by each parent's hidden Breeding Rank, a rarity tier where a lower number means a rarer, more powerful Pal. The game averages the two parents' ranks and picks the closest eligible species, so the resulting rank always falls between the two parents' own ranks.

peek: Two point pools that unlock blueprints on the tech tree.
full_text: Unlocking new blueprints runs through two separate point pools, ordinary Technology Points and Ancient Technology Points, spent on a shared tech tree. Technology Points mostly come from leveling up and from switching on new Fast Travel points. Ancient Technology Points come from defeating an Alpha Pal for the first time or beating a Tower's boss.

peek: A larger, tougher version of an ordinary Pal that acts as a roaming boss.
full_text: Alpha Pals are simply larger, tougher versions of regular Pals scattered across the map, either standing in a fixed overworld spot or waiting at the end of a Dungeon. An Alpha hands out roughly ten times the experience when defeated, takes noticeably reduced damage from every source, and is generally harder to capture. It always drops Ancient Civilization Parts on top of its usual loot.

peek: An overpowered Pal variant seen only in scripted encounters; it cannot be captured.
full_text: Predator Pals are overpowered variants of ordinary Pals that appear only in their own scripted encounters and cannot be captured. They are one of five distinct kinds of toughest fights, alongside Alpha Pals, Bounty Targets, Faction Leaders and Raid Bosses.

peek: The toughest fight: a powerful Pal summoned at your own base.
full_text: Raid Bosses are the toughest tier of fight: a powerful Pal summoned at the player's own base. They demand real preparation and base defenses to survive.

peek: A leader of a hostile faction, fought one on one inside a Tower.
full_text: Faction Leaders command hostile factions and are fought one on one inside a dedicated Tower. A Tower fight is a timed encounter: entering starts a five-minute clock, and running out of time before the boss falls gets the player killed and ejected. Up to four players can enter a Tower together.

peek: Secondary fire pulls and holds, primary fire punts.
full_text: The Gravity Gun's secondary fire pulls and holds, and its primary fire punts. Explosive barrels hit hardest, sawblades cut zombies apart, and a held radiator works as a shield you can walk behind. It will not lift most enemies, but manhacks and scanners are fair game, and thrown grenades can go back where they came from.

peek: Blind hunters that track vibration; rocks are safe, sand is not.
full_text: Antlions are blind and hunt vibration, so on the coast the rocks are safe and the sand is not. Step off and they come up.

peek: An item that makes antlions read you as a guard and swarm what you mark.
full_text: Once you have the pheropod from the Antlion Guard the antlions reverse: throw it and they read you as a guard and swarm whatever you marked. After the Antlion Guard you keep the pheropod and use antlions to break the Combine bunkers guarding the road to Nova Prospekt.

peek: Squad-based enemies that flank you while others lay down covering fire.
full_text: Combine soldiers move in squads of four to six and will flank you while the rest lay down covering fire, so holding one angle gets you surrounded. A grenade breaks them out of cover and into the open, and you can throw theirs back. Kill the shotgun one first and keep your distance from the rest; up close they club you.

peek: A launcher whose rockets you steer with its laser.
full_text: The RPG carries three rockets, and every one is steerable: hold the laser where you want it and the rocket follows, even turning right around after a miss. A gunship shoots rockets out of the air, so loop yours around behind it instead of flying it in straight.

peek: The coastal chapter that teaches the sand.
full_text: Sandtraps is the coastal chapter that teaches the sand. You go rock to rock on the way out. After the Antlion Guard you keep the pheropod and use antlions to break the Combine bunkers guarding the road to Nova Prospekt.

peek: A town where ammo is scarce and you fight with its traps.
full_text: Ammo is scarce in Ravenholm on purpose, so fight with the town instead of your guns. Levers drop car traps and reset them; waist-high blade traps shred zombies while you duck under; propane spray ignites from a single shot. Poison zombies switch traps off, so deal with those first. Loose blades are gravity gun ammunition.

peek: Three paints: blue bounces, orange removes friction, white lets you portal.
full_text: Gels are three paints, all useless on glass. Blue bounces you higher the further you fell. Orange removes friction so you keep whatever speed you arrive with. White lets you portal a surface that refused portals before, but it will not stick to cubes or turrets, and the cleansing spray strips it.

peek: The blue gel: bounce height scales with how far you dropped.
full_text: Repulsion Gel is the blue one. Bounce height scales with how far you dropped, so gain height by falling onto it from somewhere higher, not by jumping. Two coated surfaces facing each other let you climb by bouncing between them.

peek: Launches you to a fixed destination, keeping the speed you arrive with.
full_text: The Aerial Faith Plate launches to a fixed destination, but it keeps the speed you arrive with, so run or fall into one to travel further than it looks. It throws objects as well as you, and its arc can be fed through a portal.

peek: Solid light that runs until something blocks it.
full_text: A Hard Light Bridge is solid light that runs until something blocks it. Put a portal in its path to move the whole bridge somewhere else; it leaves the portal square-on, so centre the portal on the beam. It is also cover: a turret cannot see through it, let alone shoot.

peek: A beam of weightless travel that passes through portals.
full_text: An Excursion Funnel gives weightless travel along the beam. If it is carrying you the wrong way, look for the button that reverses it before assuming the route is shut. It passes through portals, so it can cross the whole chamber, and it ferries gel and cubes as well as you.

peek: The laser that feeds receptacles and relays; the exit usually needs it.
full_text: The Thermal Discouragement Beam is a laser that exists to feed receptacles and relays; the exit usually will not open until it reaches one. It goes straight through glass. Held on a turret, it cooks it.

peek: A cube that aims the laser freely.
full_text: A redirection cube aims the laser freely, while portals send it only along fixed directions. The laser exists to feed receptacles and relays.

peek: A co-op way to point at a spot or count down a timed jump.
full_text: In co-op you ping to point at a spot or to count down a timed jump; it carries without voice chat. Two players with two guns make four portals, and a portal one of you places links with the other's. Dying costs nothing but seconds.
